newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Coca-Cola opens $35 million Tanzania plant.
newsitem.headline: Coca-Cola opens $35 million Tanzania plant.

text.p: U.S. soft drinks giant Coca-Cola opened a $35 million bottling plant on Thursday in Tanzania, one of the largest investments in the impoverished East African country in years.
Coca-Cola president and chief operating officer Doug Ivester said the plant would boost economic growth and contribute to Tanzania's efforts at establishing a free-market economy.
"We will bring our knowledge, professional management and commitment. In turn the government must provide an enabling environment," Ivester said.
"This must include appropriate monetary policies and an equitable tax system."
Tanzania scrapped socialist economic policies in 1986 and with the help of foreign aid has progressively liberalised its economy and dismantled restrictive policies.
But local manufacturers complain that numerous small taxes, as well as corporate tax at 35 percent, make them unable to compete with cheap imports.
President Benjamin Mkapa has said taxation is under review.
Mkapa attended the showy gala opening of the bottling plant in Dar es Salaam and toasted its success with a glass of Coke, expressing pleasure at Coca-Cola Co's confidence in Tanzania's reforms.
"They said they make things happen, well (investments) are happening all over my country," he told reporters.

The plant, with a capacity of over 240 million bottles per year, is a joint venture between South-African based Sabco Ltd. and a Tanzanian company, IPP Ltd., whose holdings also include television and print media.
Ivester said Coca-Cola has invested over $50 million in Tanzania over the past three years, including the latest plant -- their seventh bottling plant in Tanzania and the 173rd in Africa.
Coca-Cola directly employs more than 3,500 people in Tanzania.

On Monday Coca-Cola announced plans to invest more than one billion rand ($220 million) in South Africa. The company said with further spending in other African countries it planned total investments of $500 million for sub-Saharan Africa.
One of Africa's poorest countries, Tanzania's economy is based largely on agricultural exports of coffee, tea and cotton.
